summary: Alpine County is the least populous county in California — just 1,099 residents spread across 742 square miles of Sierra Nevada high country, yielding a density of roughly two people per square mile. That's not a typo. The terrain is defined by granite peaks, volcanic ridgelines, and the upper reaches of the Carson River watershed, with much of the land sitting above 5,000 feet; annual average temperatures hover around 43°F, with overnight lows that dip to freezing year-round on average and daytime highs reaching only the mid-50s. Sunshine is generous at nine hours a day, but this is snow-country light — winters are long, cold, and isolating. There is no incorporated city in the entire county, no traffic light, no supermarket chain, and no hospital; Markleeville, the county seat, functions as the closest thing to a town center. Employment is almost entirely government and outdoor-recreation related, so switching jobs without a long mountain commute is essentially impossible. A median home value of $466,100 against a median household income near $111,000 produces a price-to-income ratio around 4.2 — manageable on paper, but the housing stock is tiny and seasonal. Alpine is a place where the grandeur of the landscape and the severity of its logistics are the same fact.
